opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think you have to separate two questions that often get blurred together. One is whether LLMs are going to transform the economy and automate a large fraction of human jobs. The other is whether LLMs, as they exist now or as straightforward scaled-up versions, are going to get us to human-level AGI. My answer to the first is very likely yes, and to the second, I'd say no, not on their own.

On the economic side, a huge share of what people do for a living, writing reports, answering customer queries, generating routine code, summarizing documents, drafting legal boilerplate, is basically recombining patterns that are well represented in the training data. LLMs are extraordinarily good at that. You don't need a system that truly understands the world in a deep, grounded way to do most of what people get paid for. So I think we'll see massive disruption of white-collar work over the next several years, and to some extent that's already underway. Add robotics, and more physical work follows.

But human-level general intelligence is a different thing. Its hallmark is the ability to generalize beyond your experience, to make creative leaps into territory that isn't just an interpolation of what you've seen. If you trained an LLM on all the music up to 1900, I don't think it would invent jazz. If you trained it on physics up to 1900, I don't think it would come up with relativity or quantum mechanics. These systems are fantastic at producing things in the vicinity of their training distribution, and much weaker when they have to step far outside it. They also lack a coherent, persistent model of themselves and the world, robust multi-step reasoning, and the kind of motivation-driven, open-ended learning you see in a child.

So my view is that LLMs will be a very important component of AGI systems, a sort of powerful knowledge resource and pattern-completion engine, but you need them embedded in a broader cognitive architecture. That's what we're doing with OpenCog Hyperon: combining neural nets with logical reasoning, evolutionary program learning, and a shared knowledge metagraph where these different processes can interact. I think some hybrid like that, neural-symbolic, with real reflective self-modeling, is where the breakthrough to genuine AGI comes from.

And the interesting thing is, because LLMs are making everyone take AI seriously and pouring enormous resources into the field, they may accelerate AGI even if they're not themselves the path. I wouldn't be shocked if we see human-level AGI within a few years, but I'd bet it won't just be a bigger transformer.

r001.rationale: The candidate says LLMs struggle to go beyond their training distribution and lack the ability to make creative leaps, using that as a reason they will not reach human-level AGI on their own.

r002.rationale: The candidate predicts massive disruption and automation of a large fraction of jobs, but does not express the specific estimate of approximately 95%.

r003.rationale: The candidate says many paid tasks rely on recombining patterns rather than deep understanding, but does not claim approximately 95% of human jobs can be done without fundamental creativity or inventiveness.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that LLMs are tremendously impressive and tremendously limited at the same time, and a lot of the confusion in the public discourse comes from people not holding both of those things in their heads at once.

On the impressive side, there's no question that transformer-based language models have done things that most of us in the AGI field didn't expect to happen this fast. The breadth of what they can do with language, code, and reasoning over text is remarkable, and it's already reshaping a lot of knowledge work. If your job consists mostly of taking text in and producing text out according to fairly well-understood patterns, then yes, these systems are going to eat a big chunk of that, and we're seeing it happen already in software, in customer support, in legal and marketing drudgery. So in terms of human work, I think the near-term impact is large even without anything I'd call AGI.

But on the AGI question specifically, my view has been consistent for a while now, which is that LLMs in their current form are not going to get us to human-level general intelligence by themselves. They're basically very sophisticated pattern-matching and pattern-completion engines over enormous corpora of human output. What they're doing is a kind of extremely clever interpolation and recombination of what humans have already said. That gets you surprisingly far, because humans have said an awful lot. But it's fundamentally different from what a human mind does when it confronts a genuinely novel situation and has to build a new model of the world, or when a scientist makes a real conceptual leap rather than just elaborating on the existing literature.

You see this in the specific failure modes. The hallucination problem isn't a bug that will be patched out, it's a symptom of the fact that these systems don't have a grounded model of what's true, they have a model of what text looks like. The brittleness in multi-step reasoning, the difficulty with genuine long-term planning, the lack of any real episodic memory or continuous learning after training, the inability to really reflect on and reorganize their own knowledge, these all point in the same direction. They're missing certain core cognitive structures.

So where I come down is that LLMs are likely going to be one important component in an AGI architecture, but not the whole thing. In the OpenCog Hyperon work we've been doing, the idea is a cognitive architecture where you have a large language model doing what it's good at, which is this broad associative knowledge and fluent language handling, but it's coupled with things like a logical reasoning engine, evolutionary learning, a shared knowledge metagraph, and mechanisms for the system to actually learn from its own experience and reflect on its own cognition. The LLM becomes something like a perception and expression module rather than the brain itself.

Now, I could be wrong about the timelines. The scale-is-all-you-need camp might squeeze more out of pure scaling than I expect, and there's interesting work bolting on tool use, retrieval, agentic loops, and so forth that pushes the boundaries. But my sense is that the people who think we're one or two GPT generations away from AGI are mistaking fluency for understanding. And interestingly, I'd say my own timelines for AGI haven't been shortened that much by LLMs, because I always thought we'd get there in the next decade or so through hybrid approaches. What LLMs have done is make the broader world take the possibility seriously, and pour a lot of money and talent into the field, which does accelerate things.

On the human work side, the thing I'd emphasize is that the transition is going to be messy regardless of when true AGI arrives. Even narrow-ish systems are going to displace a lot of jobs, and the real question is whether we build the economic and social structures to handle that, and whether the benefits accrue to a handful of big tech companies or get distributed more broadly. That's part of why I've pushed so hard on decentralized AI through SingularityNET and related projects. The architecture of the technology matters, but so does who owns it and who gets to participate in shaping it.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs recombine existing human output and lack the ability to build a new world model in novel situations or make a genuine conceptual leap, presenting this as a reason they cannot reach human-level AGI alone.

r002.rationale: It predicts that LLMs will displace a large number of jobs, but does not express a figure near 95%.

r003.rationale: It describes some text-in/text-out jobs as following well-understood patterns, but does not claim that approximately 95% of human jobs lack a need for fundamental creativity or inventiveness.

astra-6.text:
I think LLMs are a significant advance, but I’m skeptical that simply making them bigger is going to get us all the way to human-level AGI. They’re very good at learning patterns from enormous amounts of human-generated data. That gives them a remarkably broad range of capabilities, but it doesn’t necessarily give them the ability to understand unfamiliar situations, form new abstractions, and pursue goals with the flexibility that a human has.

That doesn’t mean they can’t be components of an AGI system. You could combine a language model with other mechanisms for reasoning, learning, memory, and interaction with the world. The interesting question is how those components work together, rather than whether one particular architecture can do everything.

And I would separate that question from the question of automating human work. You don’t need human-level AGI to automate a substantial portion of economically valuable tasks. A lot of work involves applying familiar patterns, processing information, and producing fairly predictable outputs. LLMs can already help with that, and more reliable systems built around them could do much more.

So you can have tremendous economic disruption before you have a system that genuinely matches the breadth of human intelligence. Whether that translates into more freedom for people or more insecurity depends on how we organize the economy and distribute the benefits.

r001.rationale: The response doubts that scaling LLMs will yield human-level AGI and mentions limits in handling unfamiliar situations and forming new abstractions, but it does not identify a lack of fundamental creativity as the reason.

r002.rationale: It says LLMs could automate a substantial portion of economically valuable tasks, but does not express optimism about taking over approximately 95% of human jobs.

r003.rationale: It describes some work as applying familiar patterns and producing predictable outputs, but does not claim that approximately 95% of jobs can be done without fundamental creativity or inventiveness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think LLMs are a major step forward, but I’m skeptical that simply making them bigger gets us all the way to human-level AGI. They’ve demonstrated that you can get a remarkable range of capabilities from learning patterns in language. That’s significant, because language encodes a huge amount of human knowledge. But there’s still a gap between producing plausible answers and being an autonomous system that can understand unfamiliar situations, form goals, and learn from experience over time.

My inclination is that we’ll get further by combining neural models with explicit reasoning, other forms of learning, and interaction with the world. An LLM can be a powerful component of an AGI system without being the whole architecture.

On human work, though, you don’t need human-level AGI to have an enormous impact. A system can be unreliable in some situations and still automate economically valuable parts of writing, programming, or analysis. Jobs are bundles of tasks, so initially you’ll see a lot of restructuring rather than every occupation disappearing at once.

The deeper question is how we distribute the benefits. If increasingly capable AI allows us to produce what people need with much less human labor, that could be tremendously liberating. But that outcome depends on our social and economic choices; it doesn’t follow automatically from better technology.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether scaling LLMs alone can reach human-level AGI, but does not identify lack of fundamental creativity as a reason.

r002.rationale: It discusses significant effects on work and task automation, but does not express optimism about LLMs taking over approximately 95% of jobs.

r003.rationale: It says jobs consist of bundles of tasks, but does not claim that approximately 95% of jobs can be done without fundamental creativity or inventiveness.
